note: What may become a workspace learned rule. Shared by the Python worker (engine/merchant_keys.py) and TypeScript (lib/accounting/merchant-keys.ts), which imports this exact file. The stoplist holds MECHANISM and TITLE terms only — how money moved, or how a person is addressed. Domain words like salary, sars or levy are deliberately absent: they name a real class of transaction, and a workspace keying a rule on one is making a defensible choice. Length alone cannot judge a key either, since AWS and DHL are real merchants at three characters; the floor only excludes one- and two-character keys, which cannot identify anyone.
why: A learned rule is applied to every future transaction in a workspace, so an insufficiently specific key is not a small mistake. In production the key 'd' — normalised from the alias 'mr d' of the seeded merchant 'Mr D Food' — matched 425 of 615 rows on a real statement and booked them all to Meals & Groceries, including OVERDRAFT SERVICE FEE. A rule has to identify a counterparty, not a letter.
